Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are the key differences between Memcached and Redis?
**Answer:** The differences span architecture, features, and use cases. **Architecture**: Memcached is multi-threaded (one process, many worker threads sharing a hash table); Redis is single-threaded for command execution (Redis 6 added I/O threading for network reads, but execution is still single-threaded). Memcached's multi-threading gives it higher raw throughput on multi-core servers (1-2M ops/sec vs ~100k for Redis per instance), while Redis's single-threading gives it simpler semantics (no locks, no races) and atomic multi-command operations. **Data model**: Memcached stores opaque blobs (just bytes, up to 1MB); Redis understands data structures (strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, hyperloglogs, streams) and operates on them server-side (push to a list, increment a hash field, fetch a sorted-set range). This makes Redis suitable for leaderboards, message queues, and rate limiters that Memcached cannot do natively (the application would have to fetch the whole blob, modify it client-side, and write it back). **Persistence**: Memcached has none (data lost on restart, by design); Redis offers RDB snapshots and AOF append-only logging for durability. **Clustering**: Memcached has no native clustering (the client does consistent hashing); Redis Cluster provides sharding with hash slots and automatic failover. **Features**: Memcached has no pub/sub, no Lua scripting, no streams; Redis has all of these. **Use case**: Memcached for pure caching (high-throughput blob storage); Redis for richer use cases (data structures, persistence, message queues). Real-world: Facebook, Wikipedia use Memcached for raw throughput; Twitter, GitHub, Slack use Redis for versatility.
**Visual:**
```
                  Memcached              Redis
  Threading:      multi-threaded         single-threaded (exec)
  Throughput:     1-2M ops/sec/instance  ~100k ops/sec/instance
  Data model:     opaque blobs (bytes)   strings/lists/hashes/sets/zsets/...
  Value size:     up to 1MB              up to 512MB
  Persistence:    none (lost on restart) RDB + AOF
  Clustering:     client-side (consistent hashing)  Redis Cluster (hash slots)
  Pub/sub:        no                     yes
  Lua scripting:  no                     yes
  Streams:        no                     yes
  Use case:       pure caching           cache + DB + MQ + leaderboard + ...
```

### Q2. Why does Memcached use a slab allocator, and what are its trade-offs?
**Answer:** The slab allocator solves the **memory fragmentation** problem that plagues traditional `malloc`/`free` allocators under mixed-size workloads. Without slabs, allocating and freeing 100-byte and 10KB values interleaved fragments memory into unusable slivers, causing the cache to use 2x its logical size and reducing hit rate (because less effective memory means more evictions). Memcached's slab allocator pre-partitions memory into **slab classes**, each holding chunks of a fixed size (class 1: 80B, class 2: 104B, class 3: 128B, etc., growing by a factor of 1.25 by default). When a `set` arrives, Memcached finds the smallest class that fits the value and stores it in a pre-allocated chunk — no `malloc`, no fragmentation, fast allocation (just pop from the free list). The trade-offs: (1) **Internal fragmentation** — a 90-byte value stored in a 104-byte chunk wastes 14 bytes (13%); if the workload's value sizes don't match the slab boundaries, this can waste 20-30% of memory. The growth factor `-f` controls this: smaller factor (1.2) means more classes (less waste, more overhead); larger factor (1.5) means fewer classes (more waste, less overhead). (2) **Slab calcification** — once a slab class is allocated, it stays that size, even if the workload shifts. If the workload suddenly has more 200-byte values but the memory is mostly 80-byte chunks, Memcached cannot reassign 80-byte chunks to 200-byte (they're different sizes). This causes premature evictions in the 200-byte class while the 80-byte class is underutilized. Modern Memcached (2.0+) has the **automove** feature to slowly rebalance slab classes, but it's conservative. (3) **Per-slab LRU** — eviction happens within a slab class, not globally, so a hot key in a full class can be evicted while a cold key in an underutilized class survives. Real-world: Facebook tunes slab sizes for their workload; most deployments accept ~15% waste.
**Visual:**
```
Traditional malloc (fragmentation):
  Alloc 100B | Alloc 10KB | Free 100B | Alloc 50B (doesn't fit in 100B hole)
  -> Memory fragmented, cache uses 2x logical size

Slab allocator (no fragmentation):
  Class 1 (80B):  [chunk][chunk][chunk][chunk][chunk]  <- values 1-72B
  Class 2 (104B): [chunk][chunk][chunk][chunk]         <- values 73-96B
  Class 3 (128B): [chunk][chunk][chunk]                <- values 97-120B
  ...
  Set "user:1" (50B value) -> Class 1, pop a free chunk, store
  Set "post:1" (90B value) -> Class 2, pop a free chunk, store
  No malloc, no fragmentation, fast allocation

Trade-off: 90B value in 104B chunk -> 14B wasted (13% internal fragmentation)
           But zero external fragmentation -> net win for most workloads
```

### Q3. How does consistent hashing work in Memcached, and why is it needed?
**Answer:** Memcached servers are **dumb** — they don't know about each other, they don't shard. The client library decides which server holds which key. The naive approach is **modulo hashing**: `server = hash(key) % N`. This works fine until the server count changes: adding a server (N -> N+1) changes `hash(key) % N` for ~100% of keys, invalidating the entire cache and causing a thundering herd of misses on the database. For a cache with 1TB of data and 100 servers, adding one server would invalidate ~990GB of cached data — a massive avalanche. **Consistent hashing** (invented by Karger et al.) solves this by placing servers on a hash ring: each server is placed at multiple points (typically 160 virtual nodes per server) on a ring of `2^32` positions. A key is hashed to a position on the ring and assigned to the next server clockwise. When a server is added, only the keys between the new server's position and the previous server's position are remapped — typically 1/N of keys, vs 100% for modulo hashing. When a server is removed, its keys are reassigned to the next server clockwise (also ~1/N of keys). The benefit: cluster scaling is graceful — adding or removing a server invalidates only a small fraction of the cache, not the whole thing. The trade-off: (1) **Slightly less even distribution** — the virtual nodes approximate but don't guarantee uniformity; some servers may get more keys than others. (2) **Client complexity** — the client must maintain the ring and handle server failures (a dead server's keys must be redistributed, with a brief cache-miss spike). The `ketama` algorithm (from Last.fm) is the canonical implementation, used by `libmemcached` and most clients. Real-world: Facebook's mcrouter, Twitter's twemproxy, and most Memcached clients use ketama-style consistent hashing.
**Visual:**
```
Modulo hashing (bad when N changes):
  N=3 servers: hash(k) % 3
    k1 -> 1, k2 -> 2, k3 -> 0, k4 -> 1, ...
  Add server (N=4): hash(k) % 4
    k1 -> 1 (same!), k2 -> 2 (same!), k3 -> 3 (CHANGED!), k4 -> 0 (CHANGED!)
  -> ~75% of keys remap (cache invalidated, avalanche risk)

Consistent hashing (graceful when N changes):
  Ring [0, 2^32):
    server1 at positions 100, 250, 400, ... (160 virtual nodes)
    server2 at positions 150, 300, 450, ...
    server3 at positions 200, 350, 500, ...

  hash(k1) = 280 -> next clockwise = server1 (at 400)
  hash(k2) = 320 -> next clockwise = server2 (at 450)
  hash(k3) = 480 -> next clockwise = server3 (at 500)

  Add server4 at positions 280, 430, 580, ...:
    k1 (hash 280) -> now server4 (at 280, was server1 at 400)
    k2 (hash 320) -> still server2 (at 450, server4 at 280 < 320 < 450)
    k3 (hash 480) -> still server3 (at 500, server4 at 430 < 480 < 500)
  -> Only ~1/N keys remap (graceful, no avalanche)
```

### Q4. Why doesn't Memcached have persistence, and what are the implications?
**Answer:** Memcached's lack of persistence is a **deliberate design choice**: Memcached is a cache, not a database, and persistence would add complexity (disk I/O, recovery logic, durability trade-offs) for a feature caches don't need. The implication: on restart (planned or crash), all cached data is lost. The application's cache miss rate spikes (the dead server's keys are now misses), but the database (the source of truth) serves them and the cache repopulates over a few minutes. The benefits of no persistence: (1) **Simplicity** — no disk I/O code, no recovery logic, no AOF rewriting, no RDB snapshots; the server is a small, easy-to-audit codebase. (2) **Performance** — no `fsync` stalls, no disk I/O on the hot path, all operations are in-memory and sub-millisecond. (3) **Operational simplicity** — no backups to manage, no persistence files to corrupt, no recovery to debug; restarts are clean (start empty, repopulate from traffic). The implications: (1) **Cache-miss spike on restart** — the application must handle a brief surge of database queries when Memcached restarts; mitigations include pre-warming the hot keys, running multiple Memcached servers (so a single restart affects only 1/N of keys), and using a circuit breaker to protect the database. (2) **Not suitable for data that must survive restarts** — sessions (if losing them logs users out), counters (if they can't be reconstructed), or any data that's expensive to recompute. For these use cases, Redis with AOF/RDB is the better choice. (3) **Treat Memcached servers as disposable** — design the system so a Memcached server can be killed, restarted, or replaced without user-visible impact. Real-world: Facebook's Memcached fleet treats each server as disposable; mcrouter reroutes traffic when a server dies, and the cache repopulates from the databases; Wikipedia's Memcached servers are restarted regularly for OS patches with no user impact.
**Visual:**
```
Memcached restart (no persistence, data lost):
  T=0    Memcached has 10M keys cached, 99% hit rate
  T=0    Restart (e.g., OS patch) -> all 10M keys LOST
  T=0    First request wave -> 100% miss -> 100% DB hit
  T=0    DB load spikes (mitigated by circuit breaker, multiple servers)
  T=0-5min Cache repopulates from traffic -> hit rate climbs 0% -> 90% -> 99%
  T=5min Steady state restored, no user-visible impact

  vs Redis with AOF (persistence):
  T=0    Redis has 10M keys, 99% hit rate
  T=0    Restart -> load AOF (replay log) -> 10M keys restored in ~30s
  T=30s  Hit rate 99% (no repopulation needed)
  -> Trade-off: AOF adds disk I/O on every write (throughput cost)
```

### Q5. What is the "slab calcification" problem, and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** Slab calcification is the problem where Memcached's slab classes, once allocated, cannot be reassigned to a different size class — even if the workload shifts and a different size class is now in demand. The scenario: at startup, Memcached sees a workload of mostly 80-byte values, so it allocates most of its memory to class 1 (80-byte chunks). Later, the workload shifts to mostly 200-byte values, which need class 5 (200-byte chunks). But class 5 has few chunks (most memory is in class 1), so class 5 fills up quickly and starts evicting LRU entries — while class 1 is mostly empty (the 80-byte values are no longer being written). The result: premature evictions in class 5 (high-value 200-byte entries evicted because the slab is full) and wasted memory in class 1 (empty chunks that can't be repurposed). The mitigations: (1) **The automove feature** (Memcached 2.0+) — a background thread monitors slab class utilization and slowly moves free chunks from underutilized classes to overutilized ones. The migration is conservative (one chunk at a time, with hysteresis) to avoid thrashing, but it eventually rebalances the slabs. Enable with `-o slab_automove` (or `slab_automove_ratio`). (2) **Pre-size the slabs at startup** — if you know the workload's value size distribution (e.g., mostly 200-byte values), configure the slab classes to favor that size (custom growth factor, or pre-allocate specific classes). This requires knowing the workload in advance. (3) **Run separate Memcached instances for different value sizes** — e.g., one instance for small JSON (100-byte values), another for large HTML (10KB values). This avoids the calcification entirely (each instance has a uniform size distribution) at the cost of more instances to manage. (4) **Use Redis instead** — Redis doesn't have slab classes (it uses a different allocator, jemalloc, which handles mixed sizes well), so it doesn't suffer from calcification. The trade-off: Redis is single-threaded (lower throughput) and has more overhead per key. Real-world: Facebook tunes slab sizes for their workload and uses automove; some deployments run separate instances per size class.
**Visual:**
```
Slab calcification:
  Startup (workload: mostly 80B values):
    Class 1 (80B):  10000 chunks (90% of memory) <- in demand
    Class 5 (200B): 1000 chunks (5% of memory)
  Later (workload shifts to 200B values):
    Class 1 (80B):  10000 chunks, 1000 used (90% empty, WASTED)
    Class 5 (200B): 1000 chunks, 1000 used (FULL, evicting LRU)
    -> Hot 200B entries evicted prematurely while 80B chunks sit empty

Mitigation: automove (slow rebalancing)
  Background thread: see class 1 underutilized, class 5 overutilized
  -> Move 1 chunk from class 1 to class 5 (slowly, over minutes)
  -> Eventually: class 1 has 2000 chunks, class 5 has 9000 chunks
  -> Class 5 stops evicting, memory utilized efficiently

Alternative: separate instances per size class
  Instance A: only 80B values -> all chunks class 1, no calcification
  Instance B: only 200B values -> all chunks class 5, no calcification
  -> More instances to manage, but no rebalancing needed
```

### Q6. How does Memcached handle concurrent access from multiple worker threads?
**Answer:** Memcached is **multi-threaded** — one process runs N worker threads (typically one per CPU core, configured via `-t`), all sharing a single hash table. The concurrency model: (1) The **main thread** runs libevent's event loop, accepts new connections, and assigns each connection to a worker thread (round-robin or least-loaded). (2) Each **worker thread** runs its own libevent event loop, processing all commands on its assigned connections. (3) Workers share the hash table, protected by **per-bucket locks** — the hash table is divided into N buckets (typically tens of thousands), each with its own lock. A worker accessing key K locks only the bucket `hash(K) % N`, not the whole table, so workers accessing different buckets run in parallel. (4) The **slab allocator** has per-slab-class locks, so workers setting values in different slab classes run in parallel. The benefit: high throughput on multi-core servers (a 32-core server can handle 1-2M ops/sec, vs ~100k for single-threaded Redis per instance). The trade-offs: (1) **Lock contention** on hot keys — if many threads access the same key (same bucket), they serialize on the bucket lock; under extreme hot-key load, throughput degrades to single-threaded levels. (2) **No atomic multi-key operations** — because operations on different keys lock different buckets, you cannot atomically update two keys (Memcached has no `MULTI`/`EXEC` like Redis). The application must use a single key (e.g., a serialized blob) for atomic multi-field updates. (3) **Per-bucket lock granularity** — if the bucket count is too low (e.g., 1000 buckets for 1M keys), many keys hash to the same bucket and contend; if too high (e.g., 1M buckets), memory overhead is high. Memcached tunes this with `hash_table_buckets` (default 65536). Real-world: Facebook's Memcached fleet runs 16-32 worker threads per server; the per-bucket locking gives near-linear scaling up to ~16 cores, after which contention reduces the gains.
**Visual:**
```
Multi-threaded Memcached (4 workers, per-bucket locks):

  Main thread: accept connection -> assign to worker 1 (round-robin)

  Worker 1: [conn A] SET k1 v1 -> lock bucket[hash(k1)%N] -> set -> unlock
  Worker 2: [conn B] SET k2 v2 -> lock bucket[hash(k2)%N] -> set -> unlock
  Worker 3: [conn C] GET k3    -> lock bucket[hash(k3)%N] -> get -> unlock
  Worker 4: [conn D] GET k1    -> lock bucket[hash(k1)%N] -> WAIT (worker 1 holds)

  Hash table (65536 buckets, each with its own lock):
    bucket[0]:    lock -> [k_a, k_b, k_c]
    bucket[1]:    lock -> [k_d, k_e]
    ...
    bucket[65535]: lock -> [k_z]

  Workers accessing different buckets -> parallel (no contention)
  Workers accessing the same bucket -> serialize on that bucket's lock
  -> Near-linear scaling up to ~16 cores, then contention reduces gains
```

### Q7. When would you choose Memcached over Redis, and vice versa?
**Answer:** The choice depends on the workload's requirements. **Choose Memcached when**: (1) **Pure caching** — you need a fast, simple key-value cache with no need for data structures, persistence, or pub/sub. Memcached's multi-threaded throughput (1-2M ops/sec per instance vs ~100k for Redis) makes it faster for raw `get`/`set` workloads. (2) **Memory efficiency matters** — Memcached's slab allocator has lower per-key overhead than Redis (which stores metadata for data structures, expiration, etc.), so for small values, Memcached fits more keys per GB. (3) **Simplicity is valued** — Memcached's tiny codebase (no persistence, no clustering, no scripting) means fewer bugs, easier auditing, and simpler operations. (4) **You're already invested in the Memcached ecosystem** — Facebook's mcrouter, Twitter's twemproxy, and the ketama consistent-hashing clients are mature and battle-tested. **Choose Redis when**: (1) **You need data structures** — leaderboards (sorted sets), message queues (lists/streams), rate limiters (counters + Lua), session stores with per-field updates (hashes). Memcached would require fetching the whole blob, modifying it client-side, and writing it back — slow and racy. (2) **You need persistence** — sessions that must survive restarts, counters that can't be reconstructed, or any data where a cache-miss spike on restart is unacceptable. (3) **You need pub/sub, Lua scripting, or streams** — Memcached has none of these. (4) **You need atomic multi-key operations** — Redis's `MULTI`/`EXEC` or Lua scripts provide atomicity; Memcached doesn't. (5) **You need clustering with automatic failover** — Redis Cluster provides this; Memcached relies on the client to handle server failures. Real-world: Facebook and Wikipedia use Memcached for pure caching; Twitter, GitHub, Slack use Redis for richer use cases. Many companies use both — Memcached for the hot path (page cache), Redis for richer features (sessions, queues).
**Visual:**
```
Choose Memcached if:
  - Pure key-value caching (no data structures needed)
  - Need max throughput (multi-threaded, 1-2M ops/sec)
  - Memory efficiency for small values (slab allocator)
  - Simplicity valued (no persistence, no clustering)
  - Already invested in mcrouter/twemproxy ecosystem

Choose Redis if:
  - Need data structures (leaderboards, queues, rate limiters)
  - Need persistence (sessions, counters that can't be lost)
  - Need pub/sub, Lua scripting, or streams
  - Need atomic multi-key operations (MULTI/EXEC, Lua)
  - Need clustering with automatic failover (Redis Cluster)

Many companies use BOTH:
  Memcached -> hot path (page cache, object cache, raw throughput)
  Redis     -> richer features (sessions, queues, leaderboards)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're caching rendered HTML fragments for a Wikipedia-like site with 10M articles. Memcached or Redis?
**Answer:** For pure HTML fragment caching, Memcached is the better choice. The reasoning: (1) **The values are opaque blobs** — rendered HTML is just bytes, no need for data structure operations. Memcached's blob storage is a perfect fit. (2) **High read-to-write ratio** — Wikipedia's articles are read millions of times per day but edited rarely; the workload is dominated by `get` operations, where Memcached's multi-threaded throughput shines. (3) **Memory efficiency** — HTML fragments are typically 1-100KB, fitting nicely in Memcached's slab classes; Redis's per-key overhead (data structure metadata, expiration tracking) would use more memory for the same data. (4) **Simplicity** — Wikipedia already runs a complex database and rendering pipeline; adding Redis's features (persistence, clustering, Lua) would add operational complexity for no benefit. The HTML cache is disposable (it can be rebuilt from the wikitext on a miss), so persistence is unnecessary. (5) **Scale** — Wikipedia's cache is enormous (terabytes of HTML), so the per-instance throughput matters; Memcached's 1-2M ops/sec per instance means fewer servers needed. The implementation: a consistent-hashing Memcached cluster (e.g., 20 servers, each 64GB), with the article URL as the key and the rendered HTML as the value. On a cache miss, the application renders the HTML from wikitext (slow, ~100ms) and writes it to Memcached with a TTL of 1 hour (so edits propagate within an hour). On edit, invalidate the cache (`delete` the key) so the next read renders fresh HTML. Real-world: Wikipedia uses Memcached for exactly this; Facebook uses Memcached for rendered page fragments.
**Visual:**
```
Wikipedia HTML cache (Memcached):
  Key: "html:en:Article_Title"
  Value: <rendered HTML, 50KB>

  Read path: GET html:en:Article_Title
    HIT  -> serve HTML (0.1ms)
    MISS -> render from wikitext (100ms) -> SET html:en:Article_Title (TTL 1h)
            -> serve HTML

  Edit path: wikitext updated -> DELETE html:en:Article_Title
    -> next read renders fresh HTML

  Memcached cluster: 20 servers, 64GB each, consistent hashing
  -> 1.28TB total cache, 20-40M ops/sec aggregate throughput
  -> Multi-threaded per server, no persistence (disposable, rebuildable)
```

### Q2. Your Memcached cluster has 10 servers. You add an 11th. How much cache is invalidated?
**Answer:** With **consistent hashing** (the default for modern Memcached clients), adding an 11th server invalidates approximately **1/11 (~9%)** of the cached keys — the keys that hash to the new server's portion of the ring. The other ~91% of keys remain on their original servers, fully cached. The explanation: in consistent hashing, each server occupies ~1/N of the ring (with 160 virtual nodes per server for even distribution). When you add an 11th server, it's placed at 160 new positions on the ring, "stealing" the keys between each of its positions and the previous server's position. The total stolen area is ~1/11 of the ring, so ~1/11 of keys are remapped. The 1/11 of invalidated keys will cause a brief cache-miss spike on the database (those keys now miss and must be repopulated from the database), but the spike is bounded to 9% of traffic, which the database can typically absorb. The contrast with **modulo hashing** (which no modern client uses, but is instructive): `server = hash(key) % N` changes for ~100% of keys when N changes, invalidating the entire cache. Consistent hashing was invented specifically to avoid this thundering-herd problem. The implementation: the client library updates its ring (adds the new server's 160 virtual nodes), and subsequent `get`/`set` operations use the updated ring. Existing keys on the old servers that didn't move are still cached (hits); keys that moved to the new server are misses (repopulated on demand). To minimize the impact, you can pre-warm the new server by proactively copying its soon-to-be-assigned keys from the database before adding it to the client's ring (advanced technique). Real-world: Facebook's mcrouter handles server additions and removals with consistent hashing; the 1/N invalidation is well-understood and rarely causes issues.
**Visual:**
```
Consistent hashing ring (10 servers, then add 11th):

  Before (10 servers, each has ~10% of ring):
    [s1][s2][s3][s4][s5][s6][s7][s8][s9][s10]
    hash(k1) -> s3, hash(k2) -> s7, hash(k3) -> s1, ...

  Add s11 (160 new virtual nodes):
    [s1][s11][s2][s3][s4][s5][s6][s7][s8][s9][s10]
         ^^^^
    s11 "steals" keys between its position and s2's position
    -> ~9% of keys (1/11) move to s11 (cache miss for those)
    -> ~91% of keys stay on their original server (cache hit)

  Modulo hashing (for contrast, NOT used):
    hash(k1) % 10 = 3 -> s3
    hash(k1) % 11 = 5 -> s5 (CHANGED!)
    -> ~100% of keys remap (entire cache invalidated, avalanche)
```

### Q3. A Memcached server in your cluster crashes. What happens, and how do you recover?
**Answer:** When a Memcached server crashes, the keys it held (1/N of the total, where N is the cluster size) are lost — they were only in that server's RAM, with no persistence and no replication. The implications: (1) **Cache-miss spike** — the keys that were on the crashed server now miss; the application falls through to the database for those keys. If the cluster has 10 servers, the crashed server held ~10% of keys, so the database sees a brief ~10% miss surge (on top of the normal ~1% miss rate). The surge is bounded by the failed server's share, so it's manageable (unlike a cache-crash avalanche, which loses all keys). (2) **Client behavior** — the client library detects the crash (TCP connection reset, timeout) and either marks the server as dead (rerouting its keys to the next server on the consistent-hashing ring) or returns errors for its keys. Most modern clients (libmemcached, pymemcache) mark the server as dead after a few consecutive failures and reroute. The rerouted keys are now misses on the new server (which doesn't have them cached), so they hit the database and repopulate the new server. (3) **Recovery** — replace the crashed server (or restart it). The client library re-adds it to the ring; its keys are reassigned back to it (another brief miss surge as the keys move back). The mitigations: (1) **Run enough servers** that losing one is a small fraction (10+ servers, so 1 crash = <10% miss surge). (2) **Use a circuit breaker** on the database to protect it during the miss surge. (3) **Pre-warm the new server** by copying its soon-to-be-assigned keys from the database before adding it to the ring. (4) **Monitor server health** and replace crashed servers quickly. (5) **Don't run with too few servers** — a 3-server cluster losing one is a 33% miss surge, which is harder to absorb. Real-world: Facebook's mcrouter handles server failures automatically, rerouting to the next server on the ring; Wikipedia's Memcached servers are monitored and replaced within minutes of a crash.
**Visual:**
```
Memcached cluster (10 servers), server 5 crashes:

  Before crash:
    s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7, s8, s9, s10 (each holds ~10% of keys)
    hit rate 99%, miss rate 1% -> DB load 1k QPS

  s5 crashes:
    s5's keys (10% of total) are LOST (in-memory, no persistence)
    Client detects s5 down (TCP reset, timeout)
    -> Marks s5 as dead, reroutes s5's keys to s6 (next on ring)
    -> s6 doesn't have those keys -> all are misses -> DB hit
    -> DB load: 1k (normal) + 10k (s5's keys repopulating) = 11k QPS (surge)
    -> Circuit breaker may trip if DB degrades

  Recovery:
    Replace s5 (or restart it) -> client re-adds to ring
    -> s5's keys reassigned back to s5 from s6
    -> Another brief miss surge as keys move back
    -> Steady state restored within minutes

  Mitigations: run 10+ servers (1 crash = <10% surge),
               circuit breaker on DB, pre-warm replacement, monitor health
```

### Q4. You're storing user sessions in Memcached. Users complain they're randomly logged out. What's happening?
**Answer:** The random logouts are likely caused by **cache eviction** — Memcached is full and evicting session keys (which logs users out when their session is gone). The diagnostic steps: (1) **Check `STAT evictions` in `stats`** — if evictions are non-zero and growing, Memcached is evicting keys due to memory pressure. (2) **Check the slab class of session keys** — sessions are typically small (100-500 bytes), so they're in a small slab class. If that slab class is full (because other small values are filling it), the LRU eviction in that class is evicting sessions. (3) **Check `STAT bytes` vs `STAT limit_maxbytes`** — if bytes is near limit_maxbytes, the cache is at capacity. The fixes: (1) **Increase Memcached memory** (`-m` flag, or add more servers) — the simplest fix, gives the cache more room so it evicts less. (2) **Tune slab classes** — if sessions are in a slab class that's full but other classes have free chunks, enable `slab_automove` to rebalance, or pre-size the slab classes for the session size. (3) **Reduce session TTL** — if sessions have a 24-hour TTL but most users only stay 30 minutes, reduce the TTL to 2 hours so sessions expire sooner (freeing memory). (4) **Don't store large values in the same Memcached** — if you're caching large HTML fragments alongside sessions, the large values consume memory that could hold sessions; use separate Memcached instances for different value sizes. (5) **Switch to Redis for sessions** — Redis's eviction policy (`volatile-lru` or `volatile-lfu`) only evicts keys with TTLs, and you can mark sessions with TTLs while persistent data has no TTL. Redis also has persistence (so sessions survive restarts). (6) **Use sticky sessions as a fallback** — pin each user to a specific server (via a load balancer cookie), so the session is only read from one Memcached server; if that server is evicted, only that user is affected (not random users). Real-world: many companies moved from Memcached to Redis for sessions specifically because of the eviction issue.
**Visual:**
```
Session eviction in Memcached:

  Slab class 3 (128B chunks, holds sessions):
    [sess:user1][sess:user2][sess:user3]...[sess:user1000]  <- FULL
    New session arrives (user1001 logs in):
    -> Evict LRU (sess:user42, who was inactive) -> user42 logged out next visit

  Diagnose:
    stats -> evictions: 5000/min (high!)
    stats -> slab 3 (128B): used_chunks 1000, free_chunks 0, evicts 5000/min
    -> Slab 3 is full, evicting sessions

  Fixes (in order):
    1. Increase -m (memory) -> more chunks for slab 3 -> fewer evictions
    2. Enable slab_automove -> rebalance from underutilized slabs
    3. Reduce session TTL (24h -> 2h) -> sessions expire sooner, free memory
    4. Separate instances for sessions vs HTML cache
    5. Switch to Redis (volatile-lru, persistence, no slab calcification)
```

### Q5. Your Memcached cluster's hit rate dropped from 95% to 70% after a deploy. What's wrong?
**Answer:** The hit-rate drop after a deploy suggests the new code is using **different cache keys** than the old code, so the existing cache entries (keyed with the old format) are now useless — every request misses. The diagnostic: (1) **Check the key format** — did the deploy change the key prefix, encoding, or hash? For example, if the old code used `user:42` and the new code uses `user:42:v2` (versioning for cache compatibility), all the old `user:42` entries are orphaned, and the new `user:42:v2` entries start cold. (2) **Check `STAT cmd_get` and `STAT get_hits`** — if `cmd_get` is normal but `get_hits` dropped, the cache is being read but the keys aren't there (different key format). (3) **Check the deploy diff** — look for changes in cache key construction (e.g., adding a version prefix, changing the serialization format). The fixes: (1) **Wait it out** — the new keys will be populated as traffic arrives, and the hit rate will climb back to 95% over a few minutes (the warm-up window). Pre-warm the hot keys to speed this up. (2) **Use cache key versioning deliberately** — if you intentionally changed the key format (e.g., to invalidate stale data after a schema change), accept the brief hit-rate drop; it's the cost of the migration. (3) **Flush the cache deliberately on deploy** — if the new code can't read the old format (e.g., the value serialization changed), flush the cache (`flush_all`) to avoid serving stale values that the new code might misinterpret. (4) **Avoid changing key formats casually** — if the change was unintentional (e.g., a refactor changed the key construction), revert it or add a compatibility layer. (5) **Use a feature flag** for cache-key changes — deploy the new code with the flag off, then enable it gradually, monitoring the hit rate. Real-world: most deploys that change cache key formats include a `flush_all` step or a key-version bump to avoid stale data; the hit-rate drop is expected and brief (5-15 minutes).
**Visual:**
```
Before deploy (old code):
  Cache keys: "user:42", "user:43", ... (10M entries, 95% hit rate)

Deploy new code (changed key format to add version):

  New code: GET "user:42:v2" -> MISS (cache has "user:42", not "user:42:v2")
  -> Falls through to DB -> SET "user:42:v2" (new key)
  -> Every request misses (cache is cold for the new keys)

  stats: cmd_get normal, get_hits low (new keys not cached yet)
  -> Hit rate: 70% (and dropping initially, before recovering)

Fix options:
  1. Wait (5-15 min) -> new keys populated -> hit rate climbs back to 95%
  2. Pre-warm: fetch top 10k hot keys, SET with new format -> faster recovery
  3. flush_all on deploy (if old keys are unusable) -> clean slate, warm up
  4. Revert key format change (if unintentional) -> old keys still valid
  5. Use feature flag -> deploy code, enable gradually, monitor hit rate
```

### Q6. You want to cache both small JSON (200 bytes) and large HTML (50KB) in the same Memcached. What are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** Mixing value sizes in Memcached exposes the **slab calcification** problem (Q5 above) and the **per-slab LRU** trade-off. The scenarios: (1) **Slab imbalance** — the 200-byte JSON values go in slab class 3 (128-byte chunks, oops, 200B doesn't fit; let's say class 6, 256-byte chunks), and the 50KB HTML goes in slab class 41 (~64KB chunks). Memcached allocates chunks to slab classes based on demand at startup, but if the workload shifts (e.g., more HTML, less JSON), the slab classes can't rebalance quickly (only the conservative `automove` is available). The result: the HTML slab class fills up and evicts while the JSON slab class is underutilized, or vice versa. (2) **Per-slab LRU eviction** — when the HTML slab class is full, Memcached evicts the LRU HTML entry, not the LRU entry globally. So a hot JSON entry that's been accessed recently survives, while a cold HTML entry is evicted — this is correct behavior (LRU within the class), but it means the eviction doesn't consider the global value of entries. (3) **Memory waste** — a 200-byte JSON value stored in a 256-byte chunk wastes 56 bytes (22%); a 50KB HTML value stored in a 64KB chunk wastes 14KB (22%). With mixed sizes, the average waste is ~15-25%. (4) **Throughput impact** — large values (50KB) take longer to serialize/deserialize and transfer over the network, so they consume more of a worker thread's time per operation, reducing the overall throughput. The mitigations: (1) **Run separate Memcached instances for different value sizes** — one instance for JSON (all small values, uniform slab usage), another for HTML (all large values). This eliminates the slab calcification (each instance has a uniform size distribution) and lets you tune the slab growth factor per instance. (2) **Use Redis instead** — Redis doesn't have slab classes (it uses jemalloc, which handles mixed sizes well), so the calcification problem doesn't apply. (3) **Compress large values** — gzip the 50KB HTML to ~5KB before storing, reducing the size disparity and the slab class needed. (4) **Tune the growth factor** — a smaller growth factor (1.2) means more slab classes, less waste, but more overhead per class. Real-world: Facebook runs separate Memcached fleets for different value sizes (small objects vs large HTML); Wikipedia separates article HTML from API responses.
**Visual:**
```
Mixed sizes in one Memcached (slab calcification risk):

  Slab classes:
    class 6 (256B):  10000 chunks, 9000 used (JSON values, hot)
    class 41 (64KB): 100 chunks, 100 used (HTML values, FULL, evicting)

  Workload shifts to more HTML:
    class 6: 10000 chunks, 2000 used (80% empty, WASTED)
    class 41: 100 chunks, 100 used (FULL, evicting hot HTML)
    -> Can't move chunks from class 6 to class 41 (different sizes)
    -> Hot HTML evicted while JSON chunks sit empty

Mitigation: separate instances per size class:
  Instance A (JSON, all 200B values):
    All chunks in class 6, no calcification, uniform slab usage
  Instance B (HTML, all 50KB values):
    All chunks in class 41, no calcification, uniform slab usage
  -> More instances to manage, but no rebalancing needed
  -> Each instance tuned for its size class (growth factor, chunk count)

Alternative: Redis (jemalloc, no slab classes, handles mixed sizes well)
```

### Q7. You're building a real-time chat application. Should you use Memcached or Redis for the message cache?
**Answer:** For a real-time chat application, **Redis is the better choice** by a wide margin. The reasoning: (1) **You need data structures beyond blobs** — chat messages involve lists (per-conversation message history), sorted sets (per-user message ordering by timestamp), and sets (conversation participants). Redis's native list and sorted set operations (`LPUSH`, `LRANGE`, `ZADD`, `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE`) are O(1) or O(log N) and atomic; Memcached would require fetching the whole conversation blob, modifying it client-side (appending a message), and writing it back — slow, racy, and bandwidth-intensive. (2) **You need pub/sub for real-time delivery** — when a user sends a message, all participants should receive it instantly. Redis's pub/sub (`PUBLISH`/`SUBSCRIBE`) fans out the message to connected clients in real-time; Memcached has no pub/sub, so you'd need a separate system (WebSocket server, Kafka) for delivery. (3) **You need persistence for message history** — chat messages are valuable (users expect to see history when they reopen the app). Redis's AOF persistence survives restarts; Memcached loses everything on restart, so message history would need a separate database, adding complexity. (4) **You need atomic operations** — appending a message to a conversation, updating the unread count, and notifying participants should be atomic. Redis's Lua scripts or `MULTI`/`EXEC` provide this; Memcached doesn't. (5) **You need Streams for consumer groups** — if you process messages with worker pools (e.g., for moderation, analytics), Redis Streams with consumer groups provide at-least-once delivery and parallel processing; Memcached lists with `LPUSH`/`BRPOP` are cruder (no consumer groups, harder to handle worker crashes). The trade-off: Redis is single-threaded (lower throughput per instance), but for chat (where each user generates ~1 message/sec, not 100k/sec), the throughput is more than sufficient. Use Redis Cluster for horizontal scaling. Real-world: Slack uses Redis for message fanout and presence; Discord uses Redis clusters for voice channel state and messaging; WhatsApp uses a custom Erlang-based system but the principles are similar.
**Visual:**
```
Chat application data model (Redis, native data structures):

  Per-conversation message list:
    LPUSH conv:42 "msg:1" "msg:2"  # append messages (newest first)
    LRANGE conv:42 0 49            # fetch latest 50 messages

  Per-user conversation list (sorted by last message time):
    ZADD user:alice:convs <timestamp> conv:42
    ZREVRANGEBYSCORE user:alice:convs +inf -inf LIMIT 0 10  # top 10 convs

  Unread count per conversation per user:
    HSET user:alice:unreads conv:42 3
    HINCRBY user:alice:unreads conv:42 -1  # mark as read

  Real-time delivery (pub/sub):
    PUBLISH conv:42:newmsg "msg:5"  # notify all participants
    SUBSCRIBE conv:42:newmsg        # participant listens for new messages

  Persistence (AOF): messages survive restart, history preserved

  vs Memcached (would require):
    GET conv:42 -> "<blob>" -> deserialize -> append msg -> serialize -> SET
    -> Slow, racy (two clients append simultaneously, one overwrites)
    -> No pub/sub (need separate WebSocket/Kafka for delivery)
    -> No persistence (need separate DB for history)
    -> More moving parts, more complexity
```
